summary: A NASA Science article reports that computer modeling by scientists at NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) suggests ancient Venus may have had a shallow liquid-water ocean and habitable surface temperatures for up to 2 billion years. The model, similar to those used for Earth climate change, showed that storm clouds formed by slow rotation and a land-heavy topography could have shielded the surface from strong sunlight. The findings were published in Geophysical Research Letters and have implications for future exoplanet missions.
one_line: NASA GISS climate modeling suggests ancient Venus may have had shallow oceans and habitable temperatures for up to 2 billion years.
key_facts: NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) modeling suggests Venus may have had a shallow liquid-water ocean and habitable surface temperatures for up to 2 billion years of its early history.
The findings were published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.
Michael Way, a GISS researcher, was the lead author of the paper.
Today Venus has a carbon dioxide atmosphere 90 times as thick as Earth's, almost no water vapor, and surface temperatures reaching 864 degrees Fahrenheit (462 degrees Celsius).
Measurements by NASA's Pioneer mission to Venus in the 1980s first suggested Venus originally may have had an ocean.
A solar day on Venus is 117 Earth days, and a sidereal day on Venus is 243 Earth days.
The GISS team postulated that ancient Venus had more dry land overall than Earth, especially in the tropics.
The model used topography from radar measurements taken by NASA's Magellan mission in the 1990s, filling the lowlands with water and leaving highlands exposed as continents.
The study factored in an ancient sun that was up to 30 percent dimmer, yet ancient Venus still received about 40 percent more sunlight than Earth does today.
Anthony Del Genio, a fellow GISS scientist and co-author, said Venus' slow spin exposes its dayside to the sun for almost two months at a time.
According to Del Genio, the resulting clouds act 'like an umbrella' and produce mean climate temperatures a few degrees cooler than Earth's today.
The research was done as part of NASA's Planetary Science Astrobiology program through the Nexus for Exoplanet System Science (NExSS) program.
The findings have direct implications for future NASA missions such as the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite and James Webb Space Telescope.
